validator: ok: no problems, soft or warnings

faults.note: The ratio step is whole: shared shaft, same speed, so the second stage starts from the slowed speed, so the ratios multiply. But the torque step jumps from 'an ideal train keeps the power the same' with no reason. Fix: one sentence that a frictionless train has nowhere to lose energy, so the work out each second equals the work in.

'Each stage is one mesh, so each one flips the direction' and the practice's 'each mesh flips it' fail for a ring gear with inside teeth and for a stage with an idler. Scope both to gears with teeth on the outside. The rule of thumb's 'raises the torque by nearly the same ratio' and 'a real box gives a little less' fail for lossy boxes such as a worm drive; say 'up to the same ratio, less what friction takes'.

faults.fault: interactive brief shows only the effect
faults.note: The brief names the cause (the two gears on the middle shaft counting the same turns) and its consequence (the second stage divides an already slowed speed), set off by turning the motor.
Read mode: no checks. Every DO screen asks him to work a figure or reason about the picture; screen 7 asks him to reason from the power bar, not recall a rule.

The two cited sources carry the two rules the lesson rests on. The torque and power trade is not in RESEARCH, so it is stated once as a textbook-standard fact and every torque figure is computed from it.
Gear names are short. The four-gear choice rows on screens 1 and 12 wrap at 360 px; screen 7's longer choices sit in a column.

faults.fault: talks about the idea instead of teaching it
faults.note: Every sentence teaches. 'That is where a winch's pull comes from, and what it costs' answers the course's opening puzzle and is followed at once by the working.
